q: The act in which people help others without any personal interest, motive, reason is called:
concept: The answer is a: helping others without any personal interest, motive or expected reward is called altruism. The word was coined by the French philosopher Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857) to mean living for others. In social psychology, altruism is helping driven purely by concern for the other person's welfare, with no expectation of reward and often at some cost to the helper. It sits inside a wider category, prosocial behaviour, which covers any voluntary act that benefits others, such as sharing, donating, comforting or rescuing, whatever the motive behind it. So all altruism is prosocial, but much prosocial behaviour is not altruistic: helping to win praise, to repay a favour or to ease one's own guilt is prosocial but self-serving. Whether pure altruism exists is a long debate. C. Daniel Batson (1981) proposed the empathy-altruism hypothesis: when we feel empathy for someone in need, we help for their sake, even when escaping the situation is easy. Robert Cialdini and colleagues (1987) replied with the negative-state relief model: we help mainly to lift our own sadness. Example: Meera sees an elderly stranger fall on a crowded Kolkata road, takes her to a clinic and leaves without giving her name; she gains nothing and loses time, so her act is altruism. Option a is right because the stem stresses the absence of any personal interest, motive or reason, which is the defining feature of altruism. Exam trap: 'prosocial' is the near-miss, because altruism is one kind of prosocial behaviour; but prosocial is the broad umbrella that also includes helping for selfish reasons, so it does not capture 'without any motive'.

traps.b: Prosocial behaviour is the broad category of any voluntary act that benefits others, whatever the motive (praise, repayment, relief of guilt); because it includes self-interested helping, it does not specifically mean helping with no motive, as altruism does.
traps.c: Nurturance is the tendency to care for and protect the young, weak or helpless; Henry Murray (1938) listed it as a psychological need (n Nurturance), so it is itself a motive, which the stem rules out.
traps.d: Social obligation is helping because a norm demands it, such as the social responsibility norm or the norm of reciprocity of Alvin Gouldner (1960); it is helping for a reason (duty), not helping without one.

q: The classification of temperament types into difficult, easy and slow to warm up was given by ________:
concept: The answer is c: the easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up temperament types were described by Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess (1977). Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, a husband-and-wife pair of psychiatrists in New York, began the New York Longitudinal Study in 1956 with Herbert Birch, following children from early infancy into adulthood. Temperament means stable, early-appearing differences in emotional and behavioural style. From parent interviews they rated nine dimensions: activity level, rhythmicity (regularity of sleep, hunger and toileting), approach or withdrawal from new things, adaptability, threshold of responsiveness, intensity of reaction, quality of mood, distractibility, and attention span and persistence. Combinations of these gave three types, described in Temperament and Development (1977). Easy children (about 40 percent) are regular, adapt quickly and are mostly cheerful. Difficult children (about 10 percent) are irregular, withdraw from new things, adapt slowly and react intensely and negatively. Slow-to-warm-up children (about 15 percent) are mildly negative and slow to adapt at first but warm up with repeated exposure. About 35 percent did not fit any type. Their key idea was goodness of fit: outcomes depend on how well the child's temperament matches the demands and patience of parents and setting. Example: on her first day at nursery, Riya clings to her mother and watches silently, but by the second week she is playing happily; she is slow to warm up. Option c is right because the three-type classification comes from Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess. Exam trap: 'James Lange' is not a person. It garbles the James-Lange theory of emotion, named after two people, William James (1884) and Carl Lange (1885), who held that bodily arousal comes before the felt emotion.

traps.a: Alfred Adler (1912) founded individual psychology and wrote on inferiority feelings and birth order; he described styles of life, not infant temperament types.

traps.d: 'James Lange' garbles the James-Lange theory of emotion of William James (1884) and Carl Lange (1885), which says we feel an emotion after perceiving our bodily changes; it has nothing to do with temperament.

q: Which of the following represents an interval level of measurement ?
concept: The answer is c: temperature measured in degrees Celsius is the classic example of an interval scale. Stanley Smith Stevens (1946) sorted measurement into four levels, remembered as NOIR: nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio. A nominal scale only names categories (gender, blood group). An ordinal scale puts things in order, but the gaps between ranks need not be equal (first, second and third in a race). An interval scale has order and equal distances between adjacent values, but its zero point is arbitrary, not a true absence of the quantity. A ratio scale adds a true zero (height, weight, reaction time, temperature in Kelvin). Celsius fits interval perfectly. The difference between 10 and 20 degrees equals the difference between 30 and 40 degrees, so adding and subtracting make sense. But 0 degrees Celsius is simply the freezing point of water, not 'no heat', so ratios do not make sense: 40 degrees is not twice as hot as 20 degrees. Example: Meera notes that Delhi was at 40 degrees and Shimla at 20 degrees. She can say that Delhi was 20 degrees warmer, but not that it was twice as hot. In psychology, IQ scores and summed Likert-scale scores are usually treated as interval data, which is why means, standard deviations and t-tests are used with them. Option c is right because Celsius has equal units but an arbitrary zero, the defining pair of features of interval measurement. Exam trap: examiners offer 'rank' or 'socio-economic status' because they involve numbers or order. Order alone makes a scale ordinal; equal intervals are what make it interval, and a true zero is what would make it ratio.

traps.a: Gender is a nominal variable: its categories are names with no order or quantity. Numbers given to them (1 for male, 2 for female) are labels only.
traps.b: Socio-economic status, as usually classified (lower, middle, upper), is ordinal: the classes are ordered, but the gap between lower and middle need not equal the gap between middle and upper.
traps.d: Rank in a competition is ordinal: it shows who came first or second, but not by how much. The winner may beat the runner-up by one second and the third-placed person by ten minutes.

q: What is the full form of the test ISAA?

options.a: Indian scale for autism in adults.
options.b: International scale for assessment of autism.
options.c: Indian scale for assessment of Autism.

concept: The answer is c: ISAA stands for the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism. It is a rating scale built in India to identify autism spectrum disorder and to grade how severe it is. The National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped (NIMH, Secunderabad, now called NIEPID, the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities) developed it in 2009, partly drawing on items of the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) of Eric Schopler and colleagues (1980). ISAA has 40 items spread over six domains: social relationship and reciprocity, emotional responsiveness, speech-language and communication, behaviour patterns, sensory aspects and the cognitive component. The clinician observes the child and interviews the parents, then rates each item from 1 (rarely) to 5 (always). Totals therefore run from 40 to 200; a total below 70 means no autism, and higher totals grade mild, moderate or severe autism with a disability percentage. This is why the scale matters in practice: ISAA is the instrument prescribed for certifying autism as a disability in India. For example, when Kabir, aged 6, is brought to a government hospital for a disability certificate, the psychologist scores ISAA, and his total decides whether he is certified and at what percentage. Option c is right because every word of the name fits: Indian (developed and standardised in India), Scale, for Assessment (it measures and grades), of Autism (the condition as a whole, not only in adults). Exam trap: each distractor changes one word, swapping "Indian" for "International" or "Assessment" for "adults"; ISAA is not an adult-only tool (it is mostly used with children), and no international scale goes by this name.

traps.a: "Indian scale for autism in adults" swaps "Assessment" for "adults"; no Indian test has this title, and ISAA is mostly used with children, not restricted to adults.
traps.b: "International scale" is wrong because ISAA was built and standardised in India by NIMH, Secunderabad (2009); the well-known foreign-origin scales are CARS (USA) and the ADOS.
traps.d: "Indian scale for adult autism" is an invented title; the two A's in ISAA stand for Assessment and Autism, and the scale is not limited to adults.

q: A key characteristic of Client-Centered Therapy is:

options.a: The therapist providing unconditional positive regard
options.b: The focus on past unconscious conflicts

concept: The answer is a: a key characteristic of client-centred therapy is the therapist providing unconditional positive regard. Client-centred (now person-centred) therapy was developed by Carl Rogers (1902 to 1987) in the 1940s and 1950s, with Client-Centered Therapy published in 1951. Rogers believed that people have an actualising tendency, an inborn drive toward growth, and that distress comes from incongruence: a gap between the self-concept and actual experience, created when love was given only under conditions of worth. The therapist does not diagnose, interpret or advise. Instead, as Rogers argued in his 1957 paper on the necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic change, the therapist offers three core conditions: congruence or genuineness, unconditional positive regard (warm, non-judgemental acceptance of the client as a person) and accurate empathic understanding, communicated through reflection of feelings. In that climate the client stops defending the self, owns denied feelings and moves toward becoming a 'fully functioning person'. Example: a student confesses that she has failed her exams and lied to her parents about it. The therapist conveys acceptance of her as a person and reflects, 'You feel ashamed and trapped between telling the truth and keeping their approval', and she begins to explore what she really wants. Option a is right because unconditional positive regard is one of Rogers's core conditions and defines the client-centred relationship. Exam trap: the other three options each name a different school (psychoanalysis, dream interpretation, CBT); in Rogers's approach the client, not the therapist, leads, and the therapist never interprets or disputes.

traps.b: A focus on past unconscious conflicts is the hallmark of psychoanalysis and psychodynamic therapy; Rogers worked with present, conscious experience in the here and now.
traps.c: Direct interpretation of dreams belongs to Freud's psychoanalysis (and Jung's analytical psychology); a client-centred therapist does not interpret at all.
traps.d: Challenging cognitive distortions is the method of Beck's cognitive therapy and CBT; Rogers's non-directive approach accepts rather than disputes the client's view.

q: How many personality disorders are mentioned in DSM-5?
concept: The answer is a: DSM-5 (2013) lists ten specific personality disorders. A personality disorder is an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from the expectations of the person's culture, is pervasive and inflexible, begins by adolescence or early adulthood, stays stable over time and causes distress or impairment. DSM-5 sorts the ten into three clusters by descriptive similarity. Cluster A, odd or eccentric: paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal. Cluster B, dramatic, emotional or erratic: antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic. Cluster C, anxious or fearful: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive. A memory aid is 'weird, wild and worried', with counts of 3, 4 and 3. DSM-5 also has personality change due to another medical condition and other specified and unspecified personality disorder, but these are not specific types. DSM-5-TR (2022) keeps the same ten, and DSM-IV also had ten. Example: Kabir is so preoccupied with orderliness, perfectionism and control that he misses every deadline; he fits obsessive-compulsive personality disorder in Cluster C. Option a is right because 3 + 4 + 3 gives ten specific disorders in the main (Section II) DSM-5 classification. Exam trap: the number 6 comes from the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders in Section III, which keeps only six specific types (antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive and schizotypal) and rates everyone else by level of personality functioning and pathological traits. ICD-11 goes further and drops the types altogether, using a single personality disorder graded mild, moderate or severe, with trait domain qualifiers.

traps.b: Eight undercounts the list: it is what you get if you forget two of the ten, for example schizotypal (Cluster A) and narcissistic (Cluster B); DSM-5 names ten.
traps.c: Nine is the usual slip of dropping one disorder, often schizotypal, which DSM-5 also lists in the schizophrenia spectrum chapter; it is still counted among the ten personality disorders.
traps.d: Six is the number of specific types kept in the Section III Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (antisocial, avoidant, borderline, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive, schizotypal), not the official Section II count.

q: Who established the first laboratory for the experimental study of psychology?
concept: The answer is c: Wilhelm Wundt established the first laboratory for the experimental study of psychology, at the University of Leipzig in Germany, in 1879. Wilhelm Wundt (1832 to 1920) was trained in medicine and physiology and wanted psychology to become an independent experimental science. In his Leipzig laboratory, students measured reaction times, sensations and feelings under controlled conditions and reported their conscious experience through trained introspection; the first dissertation from the room, Max Friedrich's study of the time needed to apperceive a stimulus, began that winter. Wilhelm Wundt had already written Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873 to 1874) and soon founded the first psychology journal, Philosophische Studien (1881). This is why 1879 is taken as the birth of scientific psychology and Wilhelm Wundt is called the father of experimental psychology. Option c is right because Leipzig 1879 is the accepted date of the first formal psychology laboratory. Exam trap: William James (1875) had a small demonstration laboratory at Harvard, which is why some sources argue for him, but it was used for teaching, not original research. Francis Galton (1884) set up an anthropometric laboratory in London to measure individual differences, and Ernst Weber (1834) gave his name to Weber's law of the just noticeable difference; both were pioneers, but neither founded the first psychology laboratory.

traps.a: Francis Galton (1822 to 1911) opened his anthropometric laboratory in London in 1884 to measure sensory acuity and reaction time in the public; he founded the study of individual differences, not the first experimental psychology laboratory.
traps.b: Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795 to 1878) was a physiologist known for the just noticeable difference and Weber's law (1834); his work came before psychology had a laboratory of its own.
traps.d: Carl Gustav Jung (1875 to 1961) founded analytical psychology (the collective unconscious and archetypes); he was a psychiatrist and clinician, not the founder of the first psychology laboratory.

q: The trait approach to personality asserts that traits are:

options.b: Discrete and discontinuous categories of people
options.c: Generalised systems which ensure consistency in an individual's behaviour
options.d: Psychological categories of temperament associated with specific body physique

concept: The answer is c: the trait approach holds that traits are generalised systems that make a person's behaviour consistent. Gordon Allport (1937), the founder of trait psychology, defined a trait as a 'generalized and focalized neuropsychic system', peculiar to the individual, with the capacity to render many stimuli functionally equivalent and to initiate and guide consistent forms of behaviour. Put simply, a trait is a real, lasting disposition inside the person that makes many different situations mean the same thing to her, so she responds to them in similar ways. Traits are continuous dimensions on which everyone can be placed, from low to high, rather than boxes. Allport grouped them as cardinal (one ruling trait that shapes almost everything), central (the 5 to 10 traits that describe someone well) and secondary (narrow preferences that appear only in some settings). Later trait theorists, such as Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck and the Big Five researchers, kept the same core idea: stable, general dispositions explain consistency across time and situations. Example: Meera is friendly at college, at a wedding and on a crowded train; her trait of sociability turns all three settings into 'chances to talk', so her behaviour is consistent across them. Option c is right because Allport's definition says exactly that traits are generalised systems guiding consistent behaviour. Exam trap: option b describes the type approach (for example, introvert and extravert as separate kinds of people), which uses discrete categories; trait theory instead uses continuous dimensions. Option d describes body-build theories, a form of type theory.

traps.b: Discrete, discontinuous categories of people are the type approach, as in Galen's four temperaments (second century AD) or Carl Jung's introvert and extravert types (1921); trait theory places people on continuous dimensions instead.
traps.d: Linking temperament to body build is the constitutional type approach of Ernst Kretschmer (1921) and of William Sheldon's somatotypes (endomorph, mesomorph, ectomorph, 1940s), not the trait approach.

q: Damage to the 'Broca's Area' of the brain is typically associated with difficulties in:
concept: The answer is d: damage to Broca's area typically produces difficulty with language production, that is, slow, effortful, non-fluent speech. Broca's area lies in the left inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45), just in front of the motor cortex region that controls the face, tongue and larynx. Paul Broca (1861) described a patient, Louis Victor Leborgne, nicknamed "Tan" because that was almost the only syllable he could produce, although he understood much of what was said to him. At autopsy Broca found a lesion in the left frontal lobe, the first strong evidence that language is localised and lateralised. Broca's (expressive, non-fluent) aphasia shows halting, telegraphic speech with content words but few grammatical words or endings (agrammatism), poor repetition, word-finding pauses, and often a right-sided weakness because the nearby motor cortex is also damaged. Comprehension of everyday conversation is relatively preserved, and patients know their speech is wrong, so they are often frustrated. Contrast Wernicke's area, described by Carl Wernicke (1874) in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus: damage there gives fluent but empty speech with poor comprehension. Example: Kabir, 62, has a left frontal stroke. Asked about his weekend he says, "Sunday... walk... dog... park," and shakes his head in frustration. When his daughter asks him to point to the window, he does so at once. Option d is right because the defining deficit after Broca's area damage is in producing speech, not in hearing or seeing. Exam trap: Broca's patients are not perfectly normal in comprehension; they struggle with grammatically complex sentences such as "The dog was chased by the cat." Even so, the textbook hallmark of Broca's aphasia is production, while comprehension is the hallmark of Wernicke's.

traps.a: Impaired language comprehension is the hallmark of Wernicke's aphasia, after damage to Wernicke's area in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Carl Wernicke, 1874), not of Broca's area damage.
traps.b: Basic auditory processing depends on the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) in the temporal lobe; Broca's area is in the frontal lobe and hearing is intact after damage there.
traps.c: Visual processing is handled by the occipital lobe (primary visual cortex, area 17) and the visual streams that run from it; it is not affected by a left inferior frontal lesion.

q: ______ is a negative emotional response or dislike towards members of a group.
concept: The answer is a: prejudice is a negative emotional response, an attitude of dislike, towards people because they belong to a particular group. Social psychologists split intergroup bias into three parts that match the ABC model of attitudes. Prejudice is the affective part (A): a feeling of dislike or hostility. Gordon Allport (1954), in The Nature of Prejudice, defined it as "an antipathy based upon a faulty and inflexible generalization". A stereotype is the cognitive part (C): a belief about the traits typical of a group, which the journalist Walter Lippmann (1922) called "pictures in our heads". Discrimination is the behavioural part (B): unfair negative action towards a group's members, such as refusing them a flat or a job. The three often travel together but can separate: a person can hold a stereotype without hostility, or discriminate because of a rule without personal dislike. Allport also ranked prejudice in action on a five-step scale, from antilocution (hostile talk) through avoidance, discrimination and physical attack to extermination. Example: Kabir believes people from another state are lazy (stereotype), feels irritated whenever one joins his office (prejudice), and never shortlists their applications (discrimination). Option a is right because the stem asks for an emotional response, and emotion is the affective component, which is prejudice. Exam trap: setters swap the three terms. Remember: stereotype is what you think, prejudice is what you feel, discrimination is what you do.

q: Vygotsky's theory of the zone of proximal development indicates that children can perform at higher level by:

options.b: Support of teachers and capable peers
options.d: Attending extra tuition classes on the subject

concept: The answer is b: Lev Vygotsky (1896 to 1934) held that children can perform at a higher level with the support of teachers and more capable peers. Vygotsky, a Russian psychologist, saw development as social: higher mental functions first appear between people and are then internalised. He defined the zone of proximal development (ZPD) as the distance between a child's actual developmental level, shown by independent problem solving, and the level of potential development, shown by problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers. The helper is called the more knowledgeable other. For Vygotsky, good teaching works inside this zone, just ahead of what the child can do alone, so that learning leads development. This contrasts with Jean Piaget (1896 to 1980), for whom development comes first and the child learns largely alone, like a little scientist. The support given within the zone was later named scaffolding by David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross (1976): help is adjusted to the child's level and withdrawn as competence grows. The idea also led to dynamic assessment: test, teach, then retest to see how much the child gains from help. Example: Riya, aged 8, can add two-digit numbers alone; with her teacher prompting 'carry the one' and an older classmate showing the steps, she manages three-digit sums. That gap is her ZPD. Option b is right because the ZPD is defined by what the child achieves with guidance from teachers and capable peers. Exam trap: option c (parents) is tempting, since a parent can be the more knowledgeable other, but it stresses support and encouragement, that is, emotional motivation, whereas the ZPD is about skilled guidance in the task itself.

q: Researchers working on a vaccine for HIV recruited over 16,000 volunteers for a study. Each volunteer was randomly assigned to receive monthly injections of either the vaccine or a placebo for a year. The researchers were curious if subjects who received the vaccine would be less likely to contract HIV than subjects who received the placebo. What is the main reason for randomly assigning the subjects?

options.a: To create groups that are as similar as possible so the main difference between the groups is the treatment
options.c: To reduce the impact of sampling variability
options.d: To ensure both the subjects and researchers are blind to who is in which group

concept: The correct answer is to create groups that are as similar as possible so the main difference between the groups is the treatment. Random assignment is the defining feature of a true experiment and the key to establishing causation. By allocating each participant to the vaccine or placebo group purely by chance, researchers ensure that, on average, the two groups are equivalent at the outset on all characteristics, both measured and unmeasured, such as age, health, lifestyle, and risk behaviour. This distributes potential confounding variables evenly across conditions, so that the only systematic difference between the groups is the treatment they receive. Consequently, if the vaccine group ends up with a lower HIV rate, that difference can be attributed to the vaccine rather than to pre-existing group differences, giving the study strong internal validity. This logic derives from the experimental design principles of Ronald Aylmer Fisher. It is essential to distinguish random assignment (used to form comparable groups and support causal inference) from random selection (used to obtain a representative sample and support generalisation). The distractors confuse random assignment with non-response control, sampling variability, and blinding, which are separate methodological issues addressed by other procedures. This item tests the core purpose of random assignment in experiments.

traps.b: Controlling non-response concerns who drops out or fails to reply; random assignment does not address non-response, so this is not its purpose.
traps.c: Reducing sampling variability relates to sample size and random selection, not to random assignment of participants to conditions.
traps.d: Blinding is achieved through the placebo and concealment procedures, not through random assignment itself; assignment can be random without anyone being blind.

q: The following test is a projective test for measurement of personality:
concept: The answer is a: the Rorschach inkblot test is a projective test of personality. Projective tests rest on the projective hypothesis: faced with an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus, people fill it with meaning drawn from their own needs, conflicts and ways of thinking. The term 'projective methods' was popularised by Lawrence Frank (1939). Hermann Rorschach (1921), a Swiss psychiatrist, published Psychodiagnostik with ten symmetrical inkblots: five in black and grey, two in black and red, and three multicoloured. In the free association phase the person says what each blot might be; in the inquiry phase the examiner asks where it was seen and what made it look that way. Responses are scored for location (whole blot or a detail), determinants (form, colour, shading, movement), content and popularity. John Exner (1974) standardised scoring in his Comprehensive System, and the newer R-PAS continues that work. Example: Arjun sees 'two people fighting over something' in several cards; a clinician would note the human movement and aggressive content and check it against other evidence before drawing any conclusion. Option a is right because the Rorschach uses an ambiguous stimulus with no right answer, the hallmark of a projective test. Exam trap: the MMPI and MCMI are personality tests too, but they are objective self-report inventories with fixed items and standard scoring. 'Personality test' does not mean 'projective test'.

traps.b: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory, by Starke Hathaway and J. Charnley McKinley (1943), is an objective true or false inventory built by empirical criterion keying. It measures personality and psychopathology, but not by projection.
traps.c: The Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory, by Theodore Millon (1977), is an objective self-report inventory aimed at personality disorders and clinical syndromes. Its fixed items and standard scoring make it objective, not projective.
traps.d: Positron emission tomography is a brain imaging method that tracks a radioactive tracer to show metabolic or blood-flow activity. It is a neuroimaging tool, not a psychological test of personality at all.

q: Which of the following is an example of primary prevention in health psychology?
concept: The three-tier scheme of prevention comes from the public-health work of Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark. Primary prevention acts before disease ever appears; its goal is to stop the illness from occurring at all by reducing exposure to risk or increasing resistance. Classic examples are immunisation, health education, clean water, and encouraging exercise or non-smoking. Promoting vaccination fits squarely here, because it protects a still-healthy person from ever contracting the disease. Secondary prevention targets the earliest, often asymptomatic, phase of disease through screening and prompt treatment, aiming to catch and reverse problems before they become serious; think mammography, Pap smears, or blood-pressure checks. Tertiary prevention comes into play once disease is established and symptomatic, and it works to limit complications, disability, and further deterioration, for example rehabilitation after a stroke or injury, or surgery and management for a chronic condition. Mapping the options onto this framework makes the answer clear: treating a diagnosed illness and operating on chronic disease are downstream, and rehabilitation after injury is the textbook illustration of tertiary prevention. Only promoting vaccination intervenes upstream on a healthy population, which is the defining feature of primary prevention. A useful memory hook is that primary prevents onset, secondary catches it early, and tertiary softens the aftermath.

traps.b: Treating a diagnosed illness is secondary or tertiary prevention because the disease is already present.
traps.c: Rehabilitation after injury is tertiary prevention, aimed at limiting disability once harm has occurred.
traps.d: Surgery for chronic disease intervenes after established pathology, making it tertiary rather than primary prevention.

q: Which of the following may occur in Expressive Language Disorder?
concept: The answer is d: limited speech, difficulty learning new words and difficulty finding the right word can all occur in expressive language disorder. Language has two sides. Receptive language is understanding what others say; expressive language is putting your own thoughts into words and sentences. In DSM-IV (1994), expressive language disorder meant that a child's expressive language was clearly below both their nonverbal intelligence and their understanding of language, enough to interfere with school or social life. Its typical signs are a small vocabulary and a limited amount of speech, short and simplified sentences, errors in grammar and tense, trouble recalling or finding words, and slowness in learning new words. Comprehension stays relatively intact, which separates it from the mixed receptive-expressive type. DSM-5 (2013) merged both types into a single diagnosis, language disorder, within the communication disorders, defined by reduced vocabulary, limited sentence structure and impaired discourse (the ability to link sentences to explain or describe something). Meera, 5, understands instructions perfectly and follows stories, but speaks in two or three word phrases, often says "that thing" because she cannot retrieve a name, and needs many repetitions to learn a new word such as "umbrella"; her hearing and intelligence are normal. Option d is right because limited speech, difficulty learning new words and word-finding difficulty are each listed features of expressive language disorder. Exam trap: do not confuse expressive language disorder with speech sound disorder (trouble producing the sounds of words) or with stuttering (trouble with the flow of speech); expressive language disorder is about vocabulary and sentence building, not pronunciation or fluency.

traps.a: A limited amount of speech is a true feature, since these children say less, in short, simple sentences; but it is only one of the listed features, so "all of these" is better.
traps.b: Difficulty learning new words (slow vocabulary growth) is also a recognised feature, so choosing it alone misses the other correct options.
traps.c: Word-finding difficulty is a classic feature of expressive language disorder too, so choosing it alone ignores the other two.

q: Which of the following was most closely associated with the structuralist school of psychology?
concept: The answer is a: Edward Titchener is the name most closely tied to the structuralist school. Edward Bradford Titchener (1867 to 1927), an Englishman, trained with Wilhelm Wundt at Leipzig and then led the psychology laboratory at Cornell University from 1892. He named the school structural psychology in his paper 'The postulates of a structural psychology' (1898), contrasting it with functional psychology. Structuralism aimed to break conscious experience into its basic elements, sensations, images and feelings (affections), describe their attributes (quality, intensity, duration, clearness) and find the laws by which they combine, much as a chemist analyses compounds into elements. Its method was trained introspection: observers were drilled to report raw sensations and to avoid the 'stimulus error' of naming the object instead. Titchener's laboratory manuals, Experimental Psychology (1901 to 1905), became standard guides. The school faded after his death, because introspective reports could not be checked and laboratories disagreed, and because it ignored children, animals, abnormal behaviour and practical use. Option a is right because Titchener founded, named and led structuralism. Exam trap: Wilhelm Wundt (who opened the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879) is often called the founder of structuralism, but Wundt called his own system voluntarism; the label 'structuralism' and the school itself belong to his student Titchener.

traps.b: William James (The Principles of Psychology, 1890) is the leading figure of functionalism, which asked what consciousness is for and how it helps us adapt, and he criticised the hunt for mental elements.
traps.c: Rene Descartes (1596 to 1650) was the 17th-century French philosopher of mind-body dualism, innate ideas and the reflex; he worked two centuries before any school of psychology existed.
traps.d: John B. Watson founded behaviourism (1913), which rejected introspection and consciousness altogether in favour of observable behaviour, the opposite of structuralism.

q: People attributing their own unwanted impulses and feelings to someone else is called:
concept: The answer is c: attributing one's own unwanted impulses and feelings to someone else is projection, an ego defence mechanism. Sigmund Freud (1856 to 1939) described defence mechanisms as unconscious ways in which the ego protects itself from anxiety caused by unacceptable id impulses or harsh superego demands, and his daughter Anna Freud (The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence, 1936) set them out systematically. In projection, a thought or feeling that would cause guilt if owned, such as hostility, jealousy or sexual attraction, is pushed out and seen in another person instead. 'I hate him' becomes 'He hates me'. Because the impulse now seems to sit outside, the person can criticise it in others without facing it in themselves. Projection is common in paranoid thinking, and George Vaillant (1977) placed it among the immature defences. Projective tests such as the Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Test rest on a related idea: people read their own needs into ambiguous material. Example: Arjun feels attracted to a colleague but believes this is wrong; instead he keeps telling friends that the colleague is always flirting with him. Option c is right because the stem defines projection exactly: one's own unacceptable feeling is attributed to another person. Exam trap: displacement (b) also moves a feeling, but it redirects a feeling the person still owns onto a safer target (shouting at a younger brother after being scolded by the boss), whereas projection changes who seems to have the feeling.

traps.b: Displacement redirects an impulse the person still owns from a threatening target to a safer one, such as kicking a door instead of hitting the boss; the feeling is not assigned to someone else.
traps.d: Denial is refusing to accept a painful external reality, such as a heavy smoker insisting there is no health risk; it rejects a fact rather than relocating one's own impulse onto another person.

q: Which area of the brain-stem controls heart rate and breathing?
concept: The answer is b: the medulla oblongata controls heart rate and breathing. The brainstem has three parts: the medulla (lowest, where it joins the spinal cord), the pons above it and the midbrain on top. The medulla holds the vital centres: the cardiovascular centre, which adjusts heart rate and blood pressure, and the respiratory centre, which generates the basic rhythm of breathing. It also runs reflexes such as swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting. These centres work automatically, so the heart keeps beating and breathing continues even in deep sleep or coma. This is why damage to the medulla is the brain injury most likely to kill, and why overdoses of alcohol, opioids or barbiturates kill mainly by silencing its respiratory centre. The medulla is also where the main motor pathways (the pyramids) cross from one side to the other, so each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. For example, if Arjun suffers a severe blow to the base of the skull and swelling presses on the medulla, doctors watch his breathing and pulse most closely, because those functions fail first. Option b is right because the vital centres for heartbeat and respiration lie in the medulla. Exam trap: the pons also helps with breathing, since its centres fine-tune the rhythm, which tempts students to pick c. But the basic, life-sustaining control of heart rate and breathing is the medulla's. The reticular formation runs through the whole brainstem core and governs arousal and alertness, not heart rate as such.

traps.d: The thalamus is a forebrain (diencephalon) relay for sensory information, not part of the brainstem, and it does not control heart rate.

q: The Zimbardo Stanford Prison Experiment demonstrated the powerful influence of:

options.d: Social roles and situational factors on behavior

concept: The answer is d: the Stanford Prison Experiment showed how strongly social roles and the situation can shape behaviour. In August 1971 Philip Zimbardo, with Craig Haney and Curtis Banks, turned a basement of Stanford University's psychology building into a mock prison. Twenty-four psychologically healthy male students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners. Prisoners were 'arrested' at home, stripped of their names and known only by numbers; guards wore uniforms and mirrored sunglasses. Within days many guards became harsh and humiliating, and the prisoners, after a brief rebellion, grew passive, distressed and helpless. The study, planned for two weeks, was stopped after six days. Because the roles were assigned at random, Zimbardo argued that the cruelty came from the role and the setting, not from the personalities of the people in them. For example, Kabir, a gentle student made a 'guard', might start shouting at 'prisoners' simply because the uniform and the rules seem to demand it. The study has been heavily criticised: there was no control group, Zimbardo himself acted as prison superintendent, and Thibault Le Texier (2019) used archive material to argue that the guards were coached to be tough. Option d is right because the lesson the study is known for is the power of roles and situational factors. Exam trap: Stanley Milgram's (1963) studies also show the power of the situation, but they concern obedience to an authority's direct commands, which is a different study.

traps.a: Obedience to authority is the subject of Stanley Milgram's (1963) shock experiments, where 65 percent of participants obeyed to 450 volts. The prison study is about people slipping into assigned roles, not about following an experimenter's direct orders.
traps.b: Groupthink is Irving Janis's (1972) account of how cohesive, insulated groups make poor decisions by suppressing dissent (the Bay of Pigs invasion). The prison study did not examine group decision making.
traps.c: The bystander effect, shown by John Darley and Bibb Latané (1968), is that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help. It concerns helping, not role behaviour in a prison.

Twenty-four psychologically healthy male students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners. Within days many guards became harsh and humiliating, and the prisoners, after a brief rebellion, grew passive, distressed and helpless. The study, planned for two weeks, was stopped after six days. Because the roles were assigned at random, Zimbardo argued that the cruelty came from the role and the setting, not from the personalities of the people in them. The study has been heavily criticised: there was no control group, Zimbardo himself acted as prison superintendent, and Thibault Le Texier (2019) used archive material to argue that the guards were coached to be tough. Option d is right because the lesson the study is known for is the power of roles and situational factors. Exam trap: Stanley Milgram's (1963) studies also show the power of the situation, but they concern obedience to an authority's direct commands, which is a different study.

q: The theory of development which emphasizes the interaction between biological predispositions and environmental experiences in shaping human behavior?
concept: The answer is d: epigenetic theory emphasises the interaction between biological predispositions and environmental experience. In developmental psychology, epigenetic theory holds that development emerges from continual, two-way traffic between genes and the environment. Its clearest statement is Gilbert Gottlieb's (1992) probabilistic epigenesis. He described four levels, genetic activity, neural activity, behaviour and the environment (physical, social and cultural), with influence flowing up and down between them. Genes do not simply issue orders: experience changes which genes are switched on, and a child's behaviour changes the environment she meets next. Development is therefore probable rather than fixed in advance. Molecular biology now shows one route. Experience adds chemical marks such as DNA methylation that alter gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. In a classic rat study, Ian Weaver, Michael Meaney and colleagues (2004) found that pups licked and groomed often by their mothers had altered methylation of a stress hormone receptor gene and grew into calmer adults. Picture Ishaan, born with a temperament that makes him wary of new people. His parents encourage him gently, and his preschool teacher pairs him with a friendly classmate. By age 6 he is still careful but socially confident: his genes set a tendency, and his experiences shaped how it was expressed. Option d is right because epigenetic theory is built on the interplay of biology and environment. Exam trap: Erik Erikson's (1950) 'epigenetic principle' is a different use of the word; it means personality unfolds through a built-in ground plan of eight stages, like organs forming in an embryo, so do not let the shared word mislead you.

traps.a: Behaviourist theory (John B. Watson, 1913; B. F. Skinner) explains development through conditioning by the environment and gives biology little role, so it is not an interaction theory.
traps.b: Maturational theory (Arnold Gesell, 1920s to 1940s) holds that development unfolds on a genetic timetable, with the environment merely supporting it; it stresses biology, not interaction.
traps.c: Sociocultural theory (Lev Vygotsky, 1934) centres on social interaction and cultural tools such as language; it accepts a biological line of development, but its focus is culture, not gene and environment interplay.

q: When same group is studied over a period of time; the study method is known as?
concept: The answer is a: a longitudinal study follows the same group of people and measures them repeatedly over a period of time. Developmental psychologists have three main designs for studying how behaviour changes with age. In a longitudinal design the same individuals are re-tested over months or years, so the researcher sees real change within each person and can test stability, such as whether a shy toddler becomes a shy teenager. The gifted children study of Lewis Terman (1921) followed about 1,500 children into old age. Its drawbacks are cost, time, loss of participants (attrition), practice effects from repeated testing, and results that may be tied to one generation. In a cross-sectional design, different age groups are tested once, at the same time; it is quick and cheap, but it confounds age with cohort (generation) effects and shows only group differences, not individual change. A sequential design (K. Warner Schaie, 1965) combines the two by following several cohorts over time; his Seattle Longitudinal Study, begun in 1956, found that most mental abilities peak in middle adulthood. Example: a researcher tests Riya and 200 other children on vocabulary at ages 5, 10 and 15 to see how each child's language grows; because the same children are tested each time, the study is longitudinal. Option a is right because studying the same group repeatedly over time is the definition of a longitudinal design. Exam trap: sequential designs also follow people over time, but they track several cohorts at once, so "same group studied over time" points to longitudinal.

traps.b: A sequential (cohort-sequential) design, set out by K. Warner Schaie (1965), combines cross-sectional and longitudinal methods by following several age cohorts over time, so it studies more than one group.
traps.c: A cross-sectional design compares different age groups at a single point in time, so different people, not the same group, supply each age.
traps.d: Recapitulation is G. Stanley Hall's (1904) theory, borrowed from Ernst Haeckel, that a child's development replays the evolution of the species; it is a theory, not a research method.

q: According to Masters and Johnson, following is the correct sequence of human sexual response:
concept: The answer is b: Masters and Johnson's sequence of human sexual response is excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution. William Masters and Virginia Johnson (1966) published Human Sexual Response after observing and measuring the bodily reactions of nearly 700 adult volunteers in the laboratory, recording heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and genital blood flow. They described a four-phase cycle, often remembered by the letters EPOR. In excitement, blood flows into the genitals (vasocongestion), the penis becomes erect, the vagina lubricates and heart rate rises. In plateau, arousal climbs further and then levels off near its peak, with rising muscle tension and faster breathing. Orgasm is the brief peak, with rhythmic muscle contractions and release of tension. In resolution, the body returns to its unaroused state; men enter a refractory period in which another orgasm is not possible, while many women can return to orgasm without one. Option b is right because it is the only option that keeps their four phase names in their true order, with plateau between excitement and orgasm rather than after orgasm. Exam trap: Helen Singer Kaplan (1979) added desire as a first phase in her triphasic model (desire, excitement, orgasm), so a sequence that opens with desire or arousal is borrowing from a later model. "Arousal" is not one of the four Masters and Johnson phase names at all; it is the everyday word for what happens across excitement and plateau. Also watch for the refractory period being slipped in as a fifth phase; it lies inside the male resolution phase.

traps.c: It replaces plateau with "arousal", which is not one of Masters and Johnson's phase names; arousal is the general process running through excitement and plateau.
traps.d: It opens with arousal and drops plateau. A phase before excitement is the idea behind Helen Singer Kaplan's (1979) desire phase, not part of Masters and Johnson's four-phase cycle.

q: Which of the following disorders is commonly associated with an "overvalued idea"?
concept: The answer is a: anorexia nervosa is the disorder most commonly associated with an overvalued idea. An overvalued idea, a term introduced by Carl Wernicke (1892), is an understandable, socially acceptable belief that comes to dominate a person's life. It is held with intense emotion and pursued far beyond reason, but, unlike a delusion, it is not held with absolute, unshakeable certainty, and it is not culturally strange: others can see why the person might think it. Unlike an obsession, it is not felt as senseless or resisted; the person agrees with it. In anorexia nervosa, the dread of fatness and the belief that one must be thin (Gerald Russell's 'morbid fear of becoming fat', 1970) is the classic overvalued idea: slimness is valued in the culture, but the patient pursues it to the point of starvation. Other examples are the preoccupation with a minor bodily flaw in body dysmorphic disorder, morbid jealousy and some hypochondriacal beliefs. Example: Riya, 17, weighs far less than is healthy for her height, yet says, 'If I eat a full meal I will become fat, and being fat would make me worthless.' She can discuss other views and is not deluded about the world, but the idea of thinness governs her days. Option a is right because the fear of fatness in anorexia is the standard textbook example of an overvalued idea. Exam trap: overvalued ideas, delusions and obsessions are easily confused; the differences are conviction (less fixed than a delusion) and ownership without resistance (unlike an obsession).

traps.b: Gender identity disorder (now gender dysphoria in DSM-5) involves a persistent experience of one's gender as different from the one assigned at birth; it is a matter of identity and distress, not the classic overvalued idea.
traps.c: Borderline personality disorder involves unstable relationships, self-image and mood, with impulsivity and self-harm; its thinking problems are stress-related paranoid ideas or dissociation, not an overvalued idea.
traps.d: Histrionic personality disorder involves excessive emotionality and attention seeking, with shallow, impressionistic speech; it is not linked with a single dominating overvalued belief.

q: An oil painting itself can include all the following cues to depth perception except:
concept: The answer is b: an oil painting can contain every pictorial depth cue, but it cannot contain retinal disparity, which needs two eyes looking at a real three-dimensional scene. The brain builds depth from cues, and only two are binocular, needing both eyes. In retinal (binocular) disparity, the eyes, about 6 centimetres apart, receive slightly different images of a near object, and the nearer the object, the bigger the difference; the brain fuses the two images into the solid depth called stereopsis. In convergence, the eyes turn inward to fixate near objects. All the other cues are monocular, and most are pictorial cues, the tools painters have used since the Renaissance: linear perspective (parallel lines such as rail tracks converge towards the horizon), texture gradient (pebbles look smaller and denser with distance), relative size (of two similar objects, the smaller image seems farther), interposition (a partly hidden object is behind), shading, height in the visual field and aerial perspective (distant hills look hazy and bluish). A flat canvas sends both eyes essentially the same image, so it carries no disparity; that is why a painting looks flatter than a real scene, and why the stereoscope of Charles Wheatstone (1838) shows each eye a slightly different picture to create disparity artificially. If Riya paints a road shrinking towards a mountain, she can use perspective, texture and size, but her painting cannot give her viewer's two eyes different views. Option b is right because retinal disparity comes from the viewer's two eyes, not from anything that can be painted. Exam trap: linear perspective, texture gradient and relative size sound technical, but they are exactly the pictorial cues a painter draws; the one binocular cue is the exception.

traps.d: Relative image size, the smaller of two similar objects seeming farther away, is a monocular pictorial cue that any painter can use.

q: The concept of inferiority complex – superiority drive was given by:
concept: The correct answer is Alfred Adler. Adler founded individual psychology and built it around the dynamic of inferiority and the striving for superiority. He proposed that all humans begin life small, weak, and dependent, producing universal feelings of inferiority. Healthy development involves compensating for these feelings through striving for competence, mastery, and ultimately what he called superiority, by which he meant self-improvement and the perfecting of oneself rather than dominating others. When this normal process is distorted, a person may develop an inferiority complex, an exaggerated, paralysing sense of inadequacy, or a superiority complex, an inflated, compensatory facade of dominance masking underlying inferiority. Adler stressed the unity of the personality, the importance of birth order and family constellation, the role of social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefuhl, a sense of community and concern for others) as the marker of mental health, and the person's unique style of life. Unlike Freud, who emphasised sexuality, Adler saw the drive to overcome inferiority and find belonging as the prime motivator of behaviour. This framework remains influential in counselling and in understanding compensation and motivation.

traps.a: Carl Jung gave us the collective unconscious and archetypes, not the inferiority-superiority dynamic.
traps.b: Victor Frankl founded logotherapy, centred on the will to meaning, not inferiority feelings.
traps.d: Erik Erikson described the eight psychosocial stages of development, including identity crisis, a separate theory.
